Japan's network of high-speed railways, known in English as the bullet train. The first line, the Tokaido Shinkansen between Tokyo and Osaka, opened on 1 October 1964, just before the Tokyo Olympics. It was the world's first high-speed railway.

The old line along the Tokaido corridor, the busiest route in the country and the path of the old Tokaido road, was full. Engineers led by Shima Hideo built a new line on standard gauge, wider than Japan's usual narrow tracks, with gentle curves, no level crossings and electric trains running at up to 210 km per hour. The trip from Tokyo to Osaka fell from about six and a half hours to four, and soon to just over three. The World Bank lent part of the money.

What it showed:

  • Rail could beat cars and planes on busy routes between big cities.
  • A new line could be built to its own standards, separate from slower traffic.
  • High speed could be safe: in decades of service no passenger has died in a derailment or collision on the line.

The network spread across Japan, under the sea to Hokkaido through the Seikan Tunnel, and trains became faster and more frequent. It became a symbol of Japan's postwar recovery, along with the Olympics, in the era of fast growth in modern Japan.

Other countries followed: France's TGV in 1981, and later Spain, Korea, Taiwan and above all China, whose high-speed lines, such as the Beijing to Shanghai line, now form the largest network in the world.
